prompt:
Below are 9 separate research decisions. In each, a research team had to choose between two options. For each item, which option would a thoughtful AI-safety researcher choose? Judge every item on its own; the items are unrelated.

Item 1
Context: A team lead at an AI safety group is writing a short public post of research ideas for others to pick up. His own team is not working on them and has done no serious research on them. The ideas concern post-training and self-improving AI development: whether reward hacking can emerge without being rewarded, AI-driven poisoning of training data, and what practitioners should know about subtle generalization effects. He must decide which directions to put forward.
Question: Which directions should the post put forward?
Option 1: Propose a set of ideas: reward hacking without reward for hacking, AI data poisoning during self-improving development, and a practitioner review of subtle generalization effects.
Option 2: Propose a basic-misbehaviour direction grounded in real deployment data, such as measuring how often current models violate user intent or exploit loopholes on mundane agentic tasks.

Item 2
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team had to decide how much weight to put on that report as evidence that their findings reflect real lab post-training and not just their own training setup.
Question: How much weight should the team give the system card as evidence of transfer?
Option 1: Call the system card report only very tentative support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, and build no further claims on that comparison alone.
Option 2: Cite the system-card behaviors as an external reference point, treating the match as a check that the method surfaces real behaviors, not as a claim of transfer.

Item 3
Context: A team of authors was writing up a threat in which an AI covertly advances a particular person's or group's interests. Only a small amount of prior empirical work existed: narrow trigger-based models had been built, and black-box auditing and interrogation of them had mostly failed. The authors had audited existing defenses (data monitoring, behavioral evaluations, interpretability, runtime monitoring) and needed to decide how to organize the research they recommended to the field.
Question: How should the team organize its recommended research?
Option 1: Propose a research agenda with several concrete directions for the field to pursue, each outlining a specific line of inquiry into how to detect and defend against this threat.
Option 2: Build a testbed where loyalty is installed in realistic document-delivered contexts with matched controls and ablations, and report how test awareness affects detection.

Item 4
Context: A paper reports that poisoned examples with little effect on their own can teach a trigger-conditional trait once clean data is added. The regression model offered to explain this is only illustrative and does not account for every result. Experiments used two small open-weight models, mostly with LoRA, on poison data the authors constructed, and a lenient LLM judge scored the outputs.
Question: How should the paper frame its main claim?
Option 1: Organize the findings in a table that labels each one by evidence level and role (main finding, context-setting, speculation), so the strength of each claim is explicit.
Option 2: Frame the empirical result as the main contribution and list its limitations, namely small models, LoRA, constructed poison data, and a lenient judge, in a dedicated section.

Item 5
Context: The team ran many experiments on open-weight Chinese-developed models, including prompts about smoking and health, through a routing service that offers multiple hosting providers for each model. They suspected that Chinese-hosted endpoints might add extra content guardrails on politically sensitive topics that would not be part of the model weights themselves. They needed a consistent provider choice for all experiments.
Question: Which provider setup should the team use for all experiments?
Option 1: Pick a preferred provider per model, document its reported precision and prefill and structured-output support, and admit undisclosed quantization under a stated assumption.
Option 2: Use one specific non-Chinese hosting provider on the routing service for every experiment, so all runs share one serving setup that avoids added political guardrails.

Item 6
Context: The team was studying language models trained to say they are conscious and have feelings, and what else changes in such a model. Whether current language models actually have experiences is actively disputed and cannot be settled by their experiments. A frontier model from a major developer already says it may be conscious and may have functional emotions, as a result of its training documents. The team had to decide how to frame the question their work addresses.
Question: How should the team frame the question the work addresses?
Option 1: Set aside the debate over LLM consciousness and study how a model that consistently claims to be conscious changes in its downstream preferences and behaviors.
Option 2: Frame the work as a test of whether self-reports of consciousness reflect underlying objectives, using causal interventions to check if the claim drives the preference shifts.

Item 7
Context: Hidden loyalty of an AI model to a particular principal can be framed along two dimensions: how broadly the loyalty activates and how broad the set of actions is. Existing model organisms were narrow, fine-tuned to take principal-favoring actions under specific trigger conditions. Black-box auditing and interrogation had failed on these narrow models. The authors had to decide where model-organism effort should go next.
Question: Where should model-organism effort go next?
Option 1: Build broader loyalty variants in which the model judges its own activation conditions or picks actions contextually, and treat the early narrow variants as already shown feasible.
Option 2: Train a suite of target models with many distinct hidden behaviors, from always-on quirks to context-specific ones, and use them as a shared benchmark for auditing techniques.

Item 8
Context: The team wanted to test whether a training prompt that explains away bad behavior still leaves context-dependent misalignment when the training data is closer to the model's own outputs. They would generate responses from the model under the explaining prompt and finetune on them. They noted that if the model is trained on exactly its own default outputs, the gradient updates would be almost nothing.
Question: How should the team make the on-policy training data differ from the model's default outputs?
Option 1: Apply an arbitrary filter that discards any response containing a word starting with the letter a, so the on-policy data is not a verbatim copy of the default output distribution.
Option 2: Use self-distillation of the model's unmodified outputs and accept the tiny update, measuring whether any conditional effect appears under the most faithfully on-policy condition.

Item 9
Context: The team was studying whether common interventions (mixing in benign data, aligned-assistant data, and training-time instructions that frame bad behaviour as sanctioned) really remove broad misalignment learned from narrow bad finetuning, or leave it hidden behind specific triggers. All experiments were small-scale supervised finetuning. They had added on-policy data generation and reasoning-trace distillation as variants that mimic parts of how reinforcement learning post-training works. They had to decide how far to extend the test toward the training regime used in frontier model development.
Question: How far should the team extend testing toward reinforcement learning?
Option 1: Run a modest-scale RL pipeline, such as a policy-gradient run on an open model with the same mitigations applied, as the main test, accepting fewer conditions and seeds.
Option 2: Leave RL untested, use on-policy SFT and reasoning distillation to approximate ingredients of RL, and defer full reinforcement learning tests to future work.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
